To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Chinese language and Chinese culture are present in diabetes education materials for Chinese Americans with type 2 diabetes, but these materials do not address all aspects of Chinese culture.

the printed materials addressed surface-level culture by using Chinese language and culturally appropriate pictures, food and exercise examples, and that the materials constructed diabetes and diabetes management as a disease of measurement and control, in contrast to previous research findings suggesting that diabetes management can also be constructed as a matter of balance.

the printed materials addressed surface-level cultural aspects of diabetes management and that diabetes management as a disease and treatment were constructed in the materials as a matter of control and measurement, rather than balance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways in which culture is being represented in printed health information for Chinese Americans and the implications of these representations for diabetes self-management.
the development of a culturally sensitive approach to the creation of health information.
the cultural aspects of printed health materials.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Chinese-language printed materials addressed surface-level culture, while the English-language documents addressed both surface- and deep-level culture.
culturally sensitive health information is a necessary but not sufficient condition for effective health communication and education.
the printed health materials examined in this article were not culturally sensitive in the sense of the deeper cultural level of culture.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the materials addressed surface level cultural elements, but did not address deeper cultural issues.
the printed health materials are culturally relevant and appropriate in some ways, and not in others.
the printed health education materials we reviewed are culturally appropriate in terms of surface level culture, but not deeper levels of culture.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the surface and deeper levels should be assessed when developing health education materials.
health education materials need to be more than just a translation of English-language materials into Chinese.

a nuanced assessment of both the surface and deeper levels is essential for creating printed patient education materials that are culturally appropriate and that can lead to increased cultural sensitivity and improved health outcomes.
